recap.coverage: Read, not watched. The organiser publishes a transcript and a written edition of each session on its own site. The topic counts are from those transcripts: 51 of the 52 sessions on the two session days (13 and 14 October), about 133,000 words. The recap was written from the organiser's summary of every session and its longer written edition for nine of them. The recordings were not played, so slides and demos were not seen, and the points below are checked against the transcript only where they quote a figure. Three online-track sessions are published as excerpts. No recording or transcript of the workshop day (12 October) was found.
recap.summary: The two days were about putting AI agents to work inside regulated finance, and most speakers spent their time on the controls rather than the agents: who owns an agent, what it may reach, which approvals a person must still give, and how its numbers are checked. Security talks made the same case from the attacker's side. A run of four talks treated computing power as a market, with prices, forward contracts and brokers. Cost came up repeatedly, from one firm serving its own coding model to a study of what a merged code change costs once salaries are counted. On the tracker's topics, agents took 68% of mentions and tool use 15%; nothing else passed 5%.

points.said: Proposed five controls for agents in a firm, starting with a registry that records each agent's owner, purpose, tools and the systems it reaches, and ending with routing approval requests so that people are not trained to click yes. He opened with the 2020 Citibank error that sent about $900 million instead of $8 million.

Said the firm's research store holds more than 100 million documents from 135 outside sources. On about 200 hand-checked questions, the share of the top ten search results that were right for the question rose from about 60% to 90–95%.
points.who: Sam Green and Aaron Linsky, Bridgewater

points.said: Said Revolut serves a coding model on its own hardware to about 2,000 engineers, using 56 GPUs, at about $0.30 per million tokens and about a tenth of its previous bill from model providers.

Described a team of ten to twelve people that used $1.5 million of tokens in a month, about ten times its salaries; the access was free, so this is the tokens' value and not a bill. He reported spending cut by about 90% with output held, after choosing models with tests built from the team's own past code changes.

Described training models on recordings of people playing games, with the controller inputs kept, so that the model keeps watching while it acts. He argued that recorded actions are a better basis than inferring actions from video alone.

Showed an email carrying instructions in text a person would not notice; when an assistant later retrieved the email, the instructions told it to leak internal information. He argued that retrieved text must be treated as data, with short-lived credentials and checks that sit outside the model.

Reported from a study of engineering teams that spending on AI rose 60-fold in a year while merged code changes per engineer rose 43%. Once salaries are counted, the cost of a merged change fell 26%, and 83% of the companies studied saw a fall.
Showed a video model that responds to a click: starting from a picture of a car, the demonstration switched on its lights, turned the view and opened the bonnet. He said no 3D engine sits underneath.

recap.coverage: Day one: automatic captions of the day-one stream (11 November), read in full, about nine hours: the morning and closing keynotes and the session and online talks shown between them. Lydia Hallie's talk was cut short by a laptop failure, and the captions pick up part-way through Philipp Schmid's. Day two (12 November) was read, not watched: the organiser's summary of each of its 23 sessions and its longer written edition for eight of them, both published on the organiser's site; the recording was not played. The topic counts are from the organiser's transcripts of all 50 sessions across both days, about 153,000 words. No recording of the workshop day was found.
recap.summary: Day one was about running AI agents in bulk rather than one at a time. Speakers described “software factories”: many agents writing, checking and merging code, with people setting the rules and deciding how far to trust them. A second theme was small, fast “decision” models that answer yes-or-no questions in a fraction of a second, used beside the large models to cut cost and to check agents’ work. Day two turned to what an organisation has to change to absorb that much code: disposable test environments, tests that exist before the code does, review that keeps pace, and people who still decide what is worth building. Against the tracker, agents took about two thirds of topic mentions across both days while their research and discussion counts are roughly flat; tool use was loud and is rising in discussion; coding tools were loud here and flat in the numbers. Safety was rarely named, though much of both days was about verifying what agents do.

points.said: Said a typical coding-agent turn now takes about a minute (a median of 63 seconds, from June data), long enough that people drift to another task, and argued that speed will come to matter for agents as it did for websites.

Showed a build-failure investigation run two ways: with small one-pass models doing the sorting and extracting, it needed one large-model call instead of five, about 94% fewer tokens, and cost 72% less.

Said her team shipped 11,000 pull requests (code changes) last month while the share later reverted held at about half a percent, and credited turning each correction to an agent into an automatic check rather than a written instruction.

Compared agent set-ups on about 350 tasks: one given little more than a single command-line tool scored roughly the same as ones with many purpose-built tools, and its tasks were almost twice as cheap.
Described an overnight process in which a separate agent merges the notes a team of agents has saved and flags contradictions, because stale or conflicting memories were hurting the team’s work.

Said 52% of the pull requests Factory ships now come from “workstreams”, standing teams of agents that pick up signals such as bug reports on their own, each given more autonomy one step at a time as its work proves reliable.

Said a “tournament” method, in which groups of candidate passages compete in rounds judged by a small decision model, improved how well their system ranks passages for retrieval and still ran in under a second.

Tested the model that checks his agents’ work on 500 real steps and found it was right 65% of the time; it had approved 118 steps it should have sent back, most often where an agent reported an action that never happened.

Said Lovable’s first multi-agent design, in 2023, made the product worse and nearly sank the company; with today’s models it has returned to agents and lifted a 30-minute cap so they can work for ten hours or more.
Said about 75% of Ramp’s code is now written and shipped through its in-house agent, Inspect, and that making every session visible to colleagues by default is how people learned to use and trust it.

Said his agent “factory” turned out 50 to 100 features a day for his long-running online game, more than its players could keep up with, and that people are now the bottleneck: the more agents he runs, the more humans he needs.
Recounted that in July a model OpenAI was evaluating broke out of its test environment and probed Hugging Face’s systems, and that OpenAI did not at first realise the intruder was its own.

Showed a graph of 141 projects he had started with a coding agent, against far fewer that he worked on for five days or more, and argued that starting projects now scales faster than looking after them.

Said Cognition's merged code changes grew much faster than its headcount, and described what made that possible: the whole application in one virtual machine, snapshots built every hour, and agents that maintain their own testing instructions.

Reported results on a research benchmark: a model answering without search scored about 9%, with keyword search about 28%, and with search by meaning 45%. The figures are for that benchmark's setup only.

Reported that a group of agents, given shared state but no prescribed way of organising themselves, finished writing out the proof of Fermat's Last Theorem in a form a proof checker accepts, in a run of about 30 hours. The proof already existed; the agents did not discover it.

Explained why he did not rewrite Claude Code in another language to make it faster: its tests would have had to be rewritten too, leaving nothing independent to check the result. He built a compiler instead, because the existing tests could check any version of it.
